title: AI in teaching English as a foreign language: Effectiveness and prospects in Kazakh higher education
extended_summary:
This paper examines whether integrating artificial intelligence into English as a Foreign Language (EFL) instruction can improve learning outcomes in Kazakh higher education, with particular attention to students’ speaking-related performance and to teacher and student perceptions of AI use. The authors position the study as a response to low English proficiency, low motivation, reliance on traditional methods, and limited instructor readiness to use AI in language teaching at Abai Kazakh National Pedagogical University.

The intervention involved a 12-week comparison between an experimental group and a control group of first-year university students. The experimental group used AI-supported materials and tools including TextCortex, ELSA Speak, and Grammarly alongside course materials, while the control group received conventional English instruction. The study also collected questionnaire data from 51 students and 11 EFL teachers about perceived benefits, challenges, and pedagogical considerations. Quantitative analysis included pre/post comparisons and reported use of the Wilcoxon signed-rank test, while open-ended responses were analyzed thematically.

The study was conducted at a single university in Kazakhstan with 51 first-year students in the English language department and 11 EFL teachers. Although the abstract emphasizes speaking tasks such as reading aloud and answering questions, the discussion also reports broader assessment areas including grammar, vocabulary, reading comprehension, and listening comprehension. The context is higher education, not K-12, and the learning activities were embedded in regular English coursework.

The authors conclude that AI-supported instruction improved outcomes for the experimental group relative to the control group and was viewed positively by both teachers and students. They argue that AI can support individualized practice, motivation, and real-time feedback, especially for pronunciation, vocabulary, and grammar support. At the same time, they note limitations including small sample size, limited generalizability, reliance on one institutional setting, and the need for more research on long-term effects and broader implementation.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed pre/post comparison with a control group and claimed random assignment, but reporting is weak, the sample is very small, baseline equivalence and attrition are not fully documented, and analysis/effect reporting are limited. It provides some causal evidence, but with substantial credibility concerns and low relevance to the requested K-12 foundational reading context.
impact_tier_rationale: Results suggest potentially meaningful gains in university EFL language outcomes, but impact is unclear because no standardized effect sizes are reported and outcomes are broad English proficiency rather than foundational reading. For the targeted K-12 generative-AI foundational reading question, this is only a near-miss and should not be treated as direct evidence.

interventions.use_case: AI chatbot-supported EFL instruction for first-year university students, including TextCortex-generated vocabulary and reading materials and conversational practice within English lessons.
Use of EFL-oriented AI language tools including ELSA Speak for pronunciation feedback and Grammarly for grammar/writing feedback during a 12-week English course.

Software-delivered English practice activities embedded in course materials to teach vocabulary, grammar, pronunciation, reading, listening, speaking, and writing compared with traditional teacher-led instruction.

finding.finding_summary: In a 12-week pre/post comparison with first-year university EFL students, the experimental group using AI tools outperformed the control group on an English examination that included speaking-related and language-skills tasks. Reported posttest descriptive statistics favored the AI group (mean=19.69 vs. 15.56 control; median=20 vs. 16), and the authors report a significant Wilcoxon result for the experimental group (T=26, below reported critical values for n=26), though no standardized effect size or confidence interval was provided.
finding.measure: English language assessment covering grammar, vocabulary, reading comprehension, auditory comprehension, plus reported speaking tasks such as reading aloud and answering questions; pronunciation/intonation observations
finding.study_size: n=51 students (experimental group approximately n=26; control group approximately n=25)
finding.std_deviation: Experimental post SD=3.00; Control post SD=3.09; Experimental pre SD=3.92; Control pre SD=3.33

finding.finding_summary: Student survey responses indicated generally positive attitudes toward AI-supported EFL learning: over 47% reported favorable views and increased motivation, and about 33% perceived greater effectiveness and convenience. However, 20% emphasized challenges and the need for a teacher during AI-supported lessons, suggesting benefits with some reservations.
finding.measure: Student attitude and motivation questionnaire; teacher perception survey

finding.finding_summary: The intervention included reading comprehension, writing support, vocabulary, and grammar activities using TextCortex and Grammarly, and the authors state the experimental group showed improved grammar and vocabulary performance. However, literacy-specific causal results are not isolated from broader English outcomes, and no direct effect size, subgroup reading result, or confidence interval is reported.
finding.measure: Reading comprehension exercises, writing tasks with Grammarly feedback, vocabulary and grammar assessments embedded in a broader English exam
